tts: This plane has one hundred eighty seats. The airline sold one hundred eighty-nine tickets. And that's not a mistake.
Airlines do it every day. It's called overbooking. Why sell seats that don't exist? And how can it pay you? That's at the end.
On every flight, somebody doesn't show up: late, sick, changed plans. That's five to fifteen percent of passengers.
And an empty seat is money gone forever: once the plane takes off, it can't be sold. So a computer predicts how many people will skip this exact flight.
But here's the catch: sometimes everyone shows up. And the gate turns into an auction: who'll fly later for a voucher? Two hundred dollars… four hundred… eight hundred.
In twenty seventeen, on a United flight, nobody took even eight hundred. So a passenger, doctor David Dao, was dragged out of his seat.
After the scandal, United raised its offer to up to ten thousand dollars. And by federal law, if you're bumped against your will, you're owed up to two thousand one hundred fifty.
Now here's what nobody tells you: that money is cash, not a voucher. Offered a voucher instead? You can say no and insist on a check. Most people never ask.
